full_title: REYNALDO A. BODO, PETITIONER, VS. COMMISSION ON AUDIT, RESPONDENT.
subject: Political and Public International Law
syllabus_topic: VII. Constitutional Commissions > B. Civil Service Commission (CSC), Commission on Elections (COMELEC), and Commission on Audit (COA) > 2. Powers, Functions, and Jurisdiction
topics: Civil liability of public officers for disallowed expenditures (Admin Code, Book VI, Sec. 43; Book I, Secs. 38-39)
Liability of the requisitioning officer who signs the purchase request
Madera Rules on Return: bad faith, malice or gross negligence required
Quantum meruit reduction of solidary liability in irregular government contracts (Torreta v. COA)
Reduction benefits solidary co-debtors who did not join the petition

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: V. Special Civil Actions > D. Review of Commission on Elections and Commission on Audit Judgments and Final Orders or Resolutions (Rule 64)

doctrine:
All government officers directly responsible for an unlawful expenditure may be held civilly liable to return the disallowed amount, from those who authorized or made the illegal payment **to those who merely took part in or contributed to it**. **But liability attaches only upon a showing of bad faith, malice or gross negligence** (Section 43, Book VI, in relation to Sections 38 and 39, Book I, 1987 Administrative Code; Rules 2a and 2b of the *Madera* Rules on Return). Applying these rules, the Court held that **a requisitioning officer who signs the purchase request may be held solidarily liable for a disallowed procurement.** A purchase request is "not a mere mechanical act." Under Section 359 of the Local Government Code, the head of the office needing the supplies must prepare it, certify that the supplies are necessary for official use, and specify the project where they will be used. The goods must be described technically, without brand names (R.A. No. 9184, Section 18). The request is one of the documents that set procurement in motion. Gross negligence or bad faith was shown here because the officer signed the request after the mayor had already approved it, and the request named a brand supplied exclusively by one contractor.

**The solidary liability under Section 43 does not necessarily equal the full disallowed amount.** When the disallowance arises from an unlawful or irregular government contract and the government received and used the goods, the liability may be reduced under the principle of *quantum meruit* (guideline 2c of *Torreta v. COA*). The contractor may keep the reasonable value of its deliveries, and that value is deducted from the disallowed amount. Fixing the quantity delivered and a fair unit price is a factual, technical matter for the COA. The reduction also benefits solidary co-debtors who did not join the petition, because their liabilities are so closely related that one cannot be fixed without affecting the other. The Court applied *Madera* and *Torreta*; it did not lay down a new rule.
facts:
In 2004, the Municipality of Barugo, Leyte directly purchased 3,900 liters of "Fil-Ocean" liquid fertilizer from Bals Enterprises for P1,950,000.00. The fertilizer was to be distributed to qualified farmers under a Department of Agriculture program. An Inspection and Acceptance Report dated May 20, 2004 acknowledged complete delivery, and the municipality distributed the fertilizer to farmers.

On December 5, 2005, COA Regional Office No. VIII disallowed the entire P1,950,000.00 for violation of R.A. No. 9184: there was no pre-bid conference, no re-bidding after the first failed bidding, and no bidding documents. The notice of disallowance (ND) held liable Mayor Juliana Villasin, municipal accountant Aluino Ala and DA technologist Gil Acuin. The Bids and Awards Committee (BAC) members were later excluded because the BAC had been bypassed. In Decision No. 2009-101 dated October 14, 2009, the COA Commission Proper upheld the ND. It found that there was no bona fide bidding: Villasin and her co-respondents had themselves conducted the alleged bidding, usurping the BAC's functions, and had specified Fil-Ocean, a brand supplied exclusively by Bals Enterprises. With no genuine failure of bidding, direct contracting had no basis. The COA also ordered a supplemental ND against petitioner Reynaldo Bodo, the municipal agriculturist, for signing the purchase request for the 3,900 liters of Fil-Ocean fertilizer.

The supplemental ND was issued on April 15, 2010. Petitioner's appeals were denied by the COA Regional Office on July 24, 2013 and by the COA Commission Proper in Decision No. 2016-316 dated November 9, 2016, which held him liable for the P1,950,000.00 disallowance. He filed a petition for certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65. He argued that, as the mere signatory of the purchase request, he had no control over or part in the decision to procure through direct contracting. He did not challenge the disallowance itself. In the COA proceedings, he had admitted that he signed the purchase request after Mayor Villasin had already approved and signed it.
issues: Whether the COA gravely abused its discretion in holding petitioner, the requisitioning officer who signed the purchase request, civilly liable for the disallowed purchase.
Whether petitioner and his solidary co-debtors are liable for the entire disallowed amount of P1,950,000.00, or whether their liability may be reduced under the principle of quantum meruit.
ruling:
Because petitioner questioned only his inclusion among the liable officers, the Court treated the disallowance and the COA's underlying factual findings as settled.

**1. No grave abuse of discretion; petitioner is civilly liable.** He may be held liable even if he did not "authorize" the direct contracting. Section 43, Book VI of the 1987 Administrative Code makes every official "authorizing or making such payment, or taking part therein" jointly and severally liable for illegal expenditures. Sections 38 and 39 of Book I protect officers who act in good faith and impose civil liability only for bad faith, malice or gross negligence, or, for subordinates, for willful or negligent acts contrary to law. Rules 2a and 2b of the *Madera* Rules on Return codify these provisions.

Petitioner's participation was undisputed. As head of the municipal agriculture office, he was the requisitioning officer who signed the purchase request. **Preparing and signing a purchase request "is not a mere mechanical act."** Under Section 359 of the Local Government Code, the head of the office needing the supplies must prepare it, certify that the supplies are necessary for official use, and specify the project where they will be used. The goods must be identified by technical description, and brand names are prohibited. The approved purchase request, together with the certifications of the budget officer, accountant and treasurer, goes to the BAC and sets procurement in motion. Petitioner's request gave "documentary support and impetus," and some appearance of legitimacy, to the sham bidding. His participation was only contributory, but it was real.

However, **liability does not rest on participation alone. It must rest on gross negligence, if not bad faith**, and the circumstances showed it. First, he signed the purchase request after the mayor had already approved it. This was a red flag, because under Sections 359 and 361 of the Local Government Code a requisition must come from the head of the requesting office before it goes up for approval. Second, the request named "Fil-Ocean," a brand supplied exclusively by Bals Enterprises. That violated the ban on brand names and showed a patent bias for one contractor, which petitioner never explained. Together these showed that he knew, or should have known, of the plan to favor Bals Enterprises. He was "utterly nonchalant" in his duties, or he actually consented to the scheme. Either way, he is liable under Section 43, Book VI in relation to Section 38, Book I.

**2. The liability may be reduced by quantum meruit, and the COA must compute it.** Solidary liability under Section 43 does not necessarily equal the total expenditure. Under the *Torreta v. COA* guidelines, when the disallowed amount arises from an unlawful or irregular government contract, the civil liability may be reduced by the amounts due the recipient under *quantum meruit* ("as much as he deserves"). Quantum meruit is an equitable device to prevent unjust enrichment. Bals Enterprises delivered the fertilizer, and the municipality acknowledged the delivery and distributed the fertilizer to farmers, so the municipality benefited. **Although the contract was invalid, Bals Enterprises may keep the "reasonable value" of its deliveries. That sum is deducted from the P1,950,000.00 disallowance, and the difference is the final liability of petitioner and his solidary co-debtors.** Fixing that value requires finding the exact quantity delivered and a fair unit price, which may differ from the contract price. The COA is better equipped for this technical task. The Court also noted an unexplained discrepancy between the 3,900 liters reported as delivered and the 2,284 liters actually distributed.

The reduction also benefits Villasin, Ala and Acuin, although they were not parties to the petition. Their liability and petitioner's are so closely related that one cannot be determined without affecting the other. The Court applied by analogy *Government v. Tizon*, on the effect of an appellate judgment on parties who did not appeal.
disposition: The petition was GRANTED IN PART. COA Decision No. 2016-316 dated November 9, 2016 was AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. The pronouncement fixing petitioner's civil liability under ND No. 10-001-101 (04) at P1,950,000.00 was VACATED. The case was REMANDED to the COA, which was directed to determine, with dispatch and in accordance with the decision, the proper civil liability of petitioner Reynaldo A. Bodo under ND No. 10-001-101 (04), and of Juliana A. Villasin, Aluino O. Ala and Gil Acuin under ND No. 05-131-101 (04).

bar_questions.q: The Municipality of San Isidro bought 500 sacks of "AgriMax" organic fertilizer through direct contracting for P2,000,000.00. The COA disallowed the payment because no genuine public bidding preceded the direct contracting: the Bids and Awards Committee was bypassed, and the mayor's staff conducted a sham bidding. The COA held liable the mayor, the accountant, and Lito, the municipal agriculturist who signed the purchase request. Lito admitted that he signed the request after the mayor had already approved it, and that the request specified "AgriMax," a brand sold only by the winning supplier. He offered no explanation for the choice of brand. Lito argues that he merely signed the purchase request and had no say in choosing the mode of procurement. Is Lito civilly liable for the disallowed amount?

alac.answer: Yes. Lito is civilly liable, solidarily with the other liable officers, because he took part in the illegal expenditure with gross negligence, if not bad faith.
alac.legal_basis: Under Section 43, Book VI of the 1987 Administrative Code, every official authorizing or making an illegal payment, or taking part in it, is jointly and severally liable for it. Under Sections 38 and 39, Book I, and Rules 2a and 2b of the Madera Rules on Return, only those shown to have acted with bad faith, malice or gross negligence must return the disallowed amount. A requisitioning officer who signs the purchase request takes part in the transaction, because a purchase request "is not a mere mechanical act" but sets procurement in motion. He is liable when he signs it after the mayor's approval, contrary to Sections 359 and 361 of the Local Government Code, and specifies a brand supplied exclusively by one contractor, contrary to Section 18 of R.A. No. 9184. (Bodo v. COA, G.R. No. 228607, October 5, 2021, En Banc)
alac.application: As head of the requesting office, Lito had to prepare the request, certify that the supplies were necessary, and describe them by technical specifications. His request gave the sham procurement its documentary basis, so his participation, though only contributory, was real. Two red flags show gross negligence or bad faith. He signed after the mayor had already approved, reversing the order the Local Government Code requires. He also specified a brand sold only by the winning supplier, without explanation. He knew, or should have known, that the supplier was being favored.
alac.conclusion: Lito is solidarily liable with the other liable officers for the disallowed amount, subject to any reduction allowed by law.

bar_questions.q: The COA disallowed the P2,000,000.00 that the Municipality of San Isidro paid, through direct contracting, for 500 sacks of fertilizer. No genuine public bidding had been held. The supplier delivered all 500 sacks, which the municipality inspected, accepted and distributed to farmers. The COA held the mayor, the accountant and Lito, the municipal agriculturist who signed the purchase request, solidarily liable to return the full P2,000,000.00. (a) May the officers' liability be reduced? (b) Suppose Lito had prepared the purchase request before the mayor approved it, described the fertilizer only by technical specifications, and knew nothing of the sham bidding later conducted by the mayor's staff. Would he still be liable to return the disallowed amount?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. The officers' solidary liability may be reduced by the reasonable value of the fertilizer delivered, under the principle of quantum meruit. (b) No. Absent bad faith, malice or gross negligence, Lito would not be civilly liable.
alac.legal_basis: (a) Solidary liability under Section 43, Book VI of the 1987 Administrative Code does not necessarily equal the full disallowed amount. When a disallowance arises from an unlawful or irregular government contract, the liability may be reduced by the amounts due the recipient under quantum meruit (guideline 2c of Torreta v. COA). If the goods were delivered and the government benefited, the contractor may keep their reasonable value, which is deducted from the disallowed amount; the COA determines that value. (b) An officer's civil liability for a disallowed transaction does not rest on participation alone. Officers who acted in good faith, in the regular performance of official functions and with the diligence of a good father of a family are not civilly liable (Sections 38 and 39, Book I, 1987 Administrative Code; Madera Rule 2a). (Bodo v. COA, G.R. No. 228607, October 5, 2021, En Banc)
alac.application: (a) The municipality accepted and distributed all 500 sacks, so it benefited from the deliveries even though the contract was invalid. The supplier may keep the reasonable value of the fertilizer. The COA must fix that value from the actual quantity delivered and a fair unit price, which need not match the contract price. That amount is deducted from P2,000,000.00, and only the difference is the officers' solidary liability. (b) In the changed facts, Lito followed the proper order for requisitions, used technical descriptions as the law requires, and knew nothing of the sham bidding. Without red flags showing bad faith or gross negligence, his participation alone does not make him liable, and the Administrative Code protects him.
alac.conclusion: (a) The liability should be reduced by the reasonable value of the delivered fertilizer as the COA determines it; (b) a requisitioning officer who acted in good faith is not liable to return the disallowed amount.

bar_questions.q: The COA Commission Proper affirmed a notice of disallowance holding Mayor Ana, Accountant Ben and Agriculturist Carlo solidarily liable for the full P3,000,000.00 paid under an irregular contract for seedlings, which the municipality received and used. Only Carlo questioned the COA decision before the Supreme Court; Ana and Ben did not. (a) What remedy should Carlo file with the Supreme Court? (b) If the Supreme Court rules that the liability must be reduced under quantum meruit, will the reduction benefit Ana and Ben, who did not join the petition?

alac.answer: (a) A petition for certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 of the Rules of Court. (b) Yes. The reduction benefits Ana and Ben as Carlo's solidary co-debtors.
alac.legal_basis: COA decisions are reviewed by the Supreme Court through a petition for certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65, on the ground of grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction. In Bodo v. COA (G.R. No. 228607, October 5, 2021, En Banc), a Rule 64 petition, the Court vacated the COA's ruling fixing the liability at the full disallowed amount and remanded the case for computation under quantum meruit. It held that the reduction may benefit solidary co-debtors who were not parties to the petition, because their liabilities are so closely related that one cannot be determined without affecting the other. The Court applied by analogy the rule on the effect of an appellate judgment when not all parties appealed (Government v. Tizon).
alac.application: (a) Carlo should file a Rule 64 petition alleging that the COA gravely abused its discretion in holding the officers liable for the entire P3,000,000.00, even though the municipality received and used the seedlings. (b) Ana, Ben and Carlo are solidarily liable for a single disallowed amount. If the Court rules that the contractor may keep the reasonable value of the seedlings, the net amount to be returned changes for all three; Carlo's liability cannot be fixed without fixing theirs. As in Bodo, where the COA was directed to recompute the liability of the mayor, accountant and technologist who did not join the petition, the reduction extends to Ana and Ben.
alac.conclusion: Carlo should file a Rule 64 certiorari petition, and any quantum meruit reduction the Court orders will also benefit Ana and Ben.

notes: Unanimous En Banc decision; Leonen, J. was on official leave. The decision relies on Madera v. COA (G.R. No. 244128, September 8, 2020) and Torreta v. COA (G.R. No. 242925, November 10, 2020). Footnote 29 cites "R.A. No. 7610" when quoting Sections 359 and 361 of the Local Government Code; the body correctly cites R.A. No. 7160. Footnote 36 calls petitioner's co-debtors "her" co-debtors, an apparent typographical slip. The 3,900 vs. 2,284 liters discrepancy comes from footnote 39 of the main opinion.
